title: "Breaking the Game" - A pilot study on the acceptance of a digital offer for young people with problematic computer game behavior - sub-study 2
summary:
Many teenagers and young adults play digital games regularly. However, some find it difficult to control their gaming time. This can lead to problems in everyday life, for example at school, in their social environment, or in family life. At the same time, people affected by computer game disorder or those showing early symptoms often shy away from seeking help from the healthcare system and look for self-help on the internet instead. However, there are currently only a few digital services that are specifically tailored to young people and have been tested for effectiveness.

“Breaking the Game” was developed to fill this gap. It is an anonymous digital service accessible via an internet browser that is aimed at young people who may be showing symptoms of computer game disorder, are avoiding seeking help from the healthcare system, and are looking for help on the internet. It provides basic information on how problematic gaming behavior can develop and encourages users to rethink their own usage behavior. Users are also encouraged to seek help from an addiction counseling center if necessary. The aim is to prevent problematic gaming behavior from becoming more severe or persisting over a longer period of time. The content is conveyed through texts, comics, and interactive elements. Among other things, it deals with how excessive gaming can develop, how personal goals can be taken into account more strongly again, how feelings can be better perceived and controlled, and what role social contacts play. 

The second sub-study examines the use of “Breaking the Game” in the setting of addiction counseling centers. The aim is to identify key issues that describe addiction counselors' perceptions of the usefulness of the intervention in their counseling practice. Based on this, recommendations for the further development and adaptation of “Breaking the Game” as an intervention tool will be developed. The following question guides the research:

• Under what circumstances do counselors from addiction counseling centers consider the use or integration of “Breaking the Game” in their everyday counseling work with young people to be useful?

Approximately ten counselors from a total of five addiction counseling centers will be interviewed twice, approximately six months apart, about their assessment of “Breaking the Game” in focus groups. The first prospective focus group will enable an evaluation of “Breaking the Game” and provide information about any necessary adjustments to the program. The second survey will retrospectively examine how “Breaking the Game” was used in everyday counseling and identify factors that promote or inhibit its integration into everyday counseling.

criteria:
Inclusion criteria:
Advisors from addiction counseling centers who advise adolescents and/or young adults aged 12 to 25 on the controlled use of digital games.
Use of “Breaking the Game” in a counseling context.

none
